analysis.one_liner: Replaces consumer bankruptcy with a simpler single chapter letting borrowers cut mortgage, car, and student loan debts.
analysis.headline: Introduced with about two weeks left in the 118th Congress and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill died there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scrap the two-track consumer bankruptcy system (Chapter 7 and Chapter 13) and replace it with one simplified chapter, "Chapter 10." Debtors could strip down mortgages on any home, rewrite car loans to the car's actual market value, wipe out student loan debt like any other debt, and get a discharge with little or no paperwork if they cannot pay anything. It would also raise fees on creditors that break consumer protection rules, and close loopholes that let wealthy debtors shield assets. It never advanced past a committee referral before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households in debt distress: people facing foreclosure or repossession, borrowers carrying student loan or credit card debt they cannot pay, and low-income filers who today must save for months to afford a lawyer. The bill's own findings name job loss, medical bills, racially disparate outcomes, and unaffordable attorney fees as the problems it targets, and it promises a discharge for debtors with no ability to pay, reduced payments when medical, child care, or housing costs are high, and easier ways to pay a lawyer.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces Chapters 7 and 13 with a single "Chapter 10" individual bankruptcy with streamlined procedures, less paperwork, and lower filing costs for routine no-payment cases.

Lets debtors modify mortgages on any residence — including reducing the loan balance and barring interest, late fees, or penalty rates on cured arrears — and rewrite car loans based on the vehicle's market value.
Makes student loan debt dischargeable on equal terms with most other debts, ending the special rule that shields most student loans from bankruptcy discharge.

Grants an immediate discharge to debtors whose calculated minimum payment obligation is $0, without requiring any plan, and lets courts reduce payment obligations when medical bills, child care, high housing costs, or care for ill or disabled family members leave the debtor unable to pay more.

Voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers on property covered by a confirmed plan, lets debtors claw back liens securing claims that get the lowest repayment priority, and raises the cost to creditors that violate consumer financial laws or the discharge injunction.
Repeals Chapter 13 entirely and closes bankruptcy loopholes the bill's findings say allow well-counseled, affluent debtors to escape repayment through asset protection planning.

analysis.who_pays: Secured and unsecured lenders. Mortgage holders would lose the current ban on modifying home loans in bankruptcy and could receive less than full contract value; auto lenders would take reduced payoffs on older cars; private student loan companies would lose the statutory shield that keeps their loans largely undischargeable; and credit card issuers and other consumer lenders would recover less through a cheaper, faster discharge system and face new penalties for abusive collection behavior. Lenders would likely argue these losses translate into higher credit costs for other borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage, auto, student loan, and card lenders

drawbacks.text: Secured lenders would recover less than they are owed under their contracts: the bill lets courts reduce home mortgage and car loan balances to property values and pay them at government-benchmark interest rates rather than contract rates, which lenders would pass on through higher rates or tighter credit for other borrowers.

Making student loans freely dischargeable could raise the price or availability of student lending going forward, a trade-off the bill itself acknowledges by arguing only that the current nondischargeability rule "has not resulted in lower financing costs" for borrowers.

The bill is a wholesale replacement of a system in place since 1978 — repealing Chapter 13 outright — which would force courts, trustees, and lenders through a major transition, and the generous discharge terms for no-payment debtors would shift losses to creditors, costs that could partially reappear in credit prices for everyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly half million households that file for bankruptcy each year, the benefits are substantial and concrete: cheaper filings, one system instead of two, the ability to save a home or car by rewriting the loan, and an escape from student debt. The costs fall on lenders whose contracts would be rewritten, and some of that cost would likely be spread to future borrowers through pricing — the honest version of the industry's objection. The bill is ambitious and would be difficult to implement cleanly, but its stated trade is explicit: easier fresh starts in exchange for lower creditor recoveries. It was never tested in either chamber, so no hearing record exists showing whether the transition concerns or the credit-cost concerns would have dominated.

outcome.mechanism: Warren dropped the bill in the last two weeks of the session; the Senate Finance Committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Consumer Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2024 on December 18, 2024, the final stretch of the 118th Congress, with Senator Sheldon Whitehouse as the bill's one cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — its only action of the Congress.
The Finance Committee held no hearing, took no markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor; Congress adjourned on January 3, 2025, ending the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Secured lenders — mortgage holders, auto finance companies, and private student loan companies — keep the current rules that let them collect full contract value, block mortgage modification, and keep student loans nearly impossible to discharge. Affluent debtors skilled at asset protection also keep the loopholes the bill would have closed.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored the bill and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of a full fight never got a chance to show itself — though the bill carried the 48-vote Democratic side only.

industries.note: The bill repeals the longstanding ban on reducing home mortgage balances in bankruptcy, letting debtors rewrite loans and cure defaults without penalty interest or late fees. It would cut recoveries on the largest consumer loan market in the country.

Car loans could be rewritten to the vehicle's market value, ending the rule that forces debtors to repay the full loan even on cars worth far less. Lenders would absorb the difference on most repossessed or underwater cars.

Student debt would be dischargeable on equal terms with other consumer debt, removing the statutory shield that has made these loans nearly impossible to walk away from. The bill notes the shield never lowered borrowers' financing costs.

A single cheap, fast bankruptcy chapter with automatic discharges for no-payment debtors would cut what these lenders recover, and new enforcement provisions add penalties for creditors that violate consumer financial laws or the discharge injunction.

The bill rules that rent-to-own companies hold no property interest in the goods, caps what they can collect in a case, and voids their rights after discharge — stripping a legal structure the industry relies on.

By cutting paperwork and letting debtors pay attorneys through the plan, the bill aims to make counsel affordable for people who now save for months to file. Trustees keep their role in the new chapter and fee provisions are reworked in Title IV.
